newsitem.title: USA: Clinton unveils tax simplification proposals.
newsitem.headline: Clinton unveils tax simplification proposals.

text.p: The Clinton administration Monday unveiled some 60 tax simplifications proposals it said would make it easier for both families and small business to complete and file their returns.
If enacted by Congress, the measures will simplify the incredibly complex tax code without increasing or reducing taxes, the administration said.

"The task of filing taxes has become too complex for too many families," President Clinton said in a statement. "This tax simplification plan will begin to ease that burden, particularly for families with children and for small business."
The proposals come just one day before Americans must file their tax returns and pay whatever they still owe for last year.

The complex changes to the huge tax code, if adopted, would increase the standard deduction to unearned income to so-called dependent filers as well as excluding more than 2 million corporations from calculating the so-called alternative minimum tax.
The Treasury estimated that the dependent provision would free some 1.7 million people, mostly children, from having to file a separate tax return.

In addition, the corporate proposal would exempt busnesses with annual gross income below $5 million from dealing with the part of the tax code desinged to ensure that companies pay some minimum tax even if they claim substantial deductions.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the government will seek ways to move to an electronic tax payment system that would permit taxpayers to pay their liabilities using credit card, debit card or other forms of electronic fund transfers.
"Our goal is clear, we want to make life easier for the American taxpayer," Rubin told a briefing for reporters.
The proposals came under immediate fire from Repulicans on Capitol Hill, who argued that the best way for the administration to simplify the system would be to cut spending.

"While I applaud the step taken today by the administration in tax simplification, I am concerned that it is only giving an aspirin to a patient who needs a heart transplant," said Sen. William Roth, a Deleware Republican who chairs the powerful Finance Committee.
